issues.description: The Methods section explicitly states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with a mean age of 19 and n=374, characteristics typical of a student convenience sample. Yet the paper consistently claims throughout the abstract, introduction, results, and discussion to use a 'national probability sample' and 'general population sample.' These are mutually exclusive characterizations. A university intro-psych pool is by definition not a national probability sample. The paper also instructs readers to see 'the NZAVS website' for full sample details, but the NZAVS is a nationally-representative panel with thousands of participants—not a 374-person student pool. This contradiction undermines the entire framing and comparative logic of the study.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The paper consistently labels the outcome variable as 'willingness to change behaviour to benefit the environment' (abstract), 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' (results and discussion), and 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment' (Figure 1 caption and throughout). However, the actual items described in the Measures section assess environmental concern ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'). Concern and behavioral willingness/sacrifice are conceptually and empirically distinct constructs. The measure operationalises an affective/cognitive appraisal, not a behavioral intention or sacrifice. This mislabeling affects the validity of all theoretical interpretations and the stated conclusions.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'.

issues.description: The Strengths and Limitations section states 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' Given that the Methods describes an introductory psychology participant pool at a single university (n=374, mean age 19, 68% female, 86% Pākehā), this claim is empirically false. An intro-psych convenience sample is not nationally representative by any standard definition. This false claim of generalizability will mislead readers and inflates the perceived external validity of the findings. All generalizations to the 'general population' throughout the Discussion are similarly unwarranted.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The reported RMSEA confidence interval of 90% CI [.025, .026] spans only .001 units, which is implausibly narrow for any structural equation model and is effectively a point estimate rather than an interval. More critically, the interval [.025, .026] does not contain the stated RMSEA point estimate of .03, which is a logical impossibility—a confidence interval must contain the point estimate it is derived from. This strongly suggests a typographical or computational error (likely the upper bound should be .035 or similar). As the RMSEA is one of the primary justifications for accepting the model, this error is consequential for evaluating model fit.
issues.quote: those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference test for comparing the SDO→RWA and RWA→SDO cross-lagged paths yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square difference value of over 15,000 for a 1 df test is extraordinarily implausible in a standard path model of this size and complexity. For context, the entire model chi-square is χ²(2279) = 36,511.73. A single parameter-equality constraint producing a Δχ² equal to 42% of the full-model chi-square is not credible and strongly suggests a computational error, possibly resulting from a software input error, incorrect degrees of freedom, or misreporting of results.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.subcategory: missing scale item compromises measurement invariance
issues.description: The paper acknowledges that one of the six RWA items ('Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the 'normal way' things are supposed to be done') was not administered at Time 2. The cross-lagged model constrains parameters to be time-invariant (stationary), which requires strict measurement equivalence across time points. Administering a different item set at one time point means the latent RWA construct at T2 is measured by a different (and differently balanced) five-item set, violating the fundamental assumption of measurement invariance. The authors do not acknowledge this problem, do not test for measurement invariance, and do not discuss what effect this might have on the constrained T1-to-T2 and T2-to-T3 lagged paths involving RWA.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: poor model fit accepted without justification
issues.description: The authors report a CFI of .86 and note that 'model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity,' but proceed to accept the model based selectively on the RMSEA and SRMR. A CFI of .86 falls below the widely accepted thresholds of .90 (adequate) and .95 (good fit). While it is true that CFI is sensitive to model complexity, dismissing it without formal justification or sensitivity analysis is methodologically problematic. Furthermore, the chi-square ratio (36511.73 / 2279 ≈ 16) is extremely high. The authors provide no discussion of what the poor CFI implies for the model's accuracy in reproducing the observed covariance structure, nor do they consider more parsimonious alternative models.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: unwarranted causal claims from longitudinal correlational design
issues.description: The Discussion repeatedly makes strong causal claims that are not warranted by a cross-lagged panel model. Phrases such as 'a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism,' 'SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes,' and 'the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future' imply experimental or quasi-experimental evidence. Cross-lagged panel models establish temporal precedence of association while controlling for prior levels, but they do not rule out unmeasured confounders, reverse causation in unmeasured variables, or third-variable explanations. The authors themselves acknowledge a possible third-variable explanation in the Discussion but then proceed to make strong causal statements in the Conclusion.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.

issues.subcategory: non-significant model comparison used to assert differential prediction
issues.description: The authors constrain the SDO→environmentalism and RWA→environmentalism paths to equality and compare fit to the freely estimated model, obtaining χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126. This non-significant result means the hypothesis that SDO and RWA are equally strong predictors cannot be rejected at the stated p < .05 threshold. Despite this, the authors conclude 'we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.' This is a logical inconsistency: the formal test they designed to evaluate this question fails to support the claim, yet they assert it anyway based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients. This practice of conducting a formal test, finding it non-significant, and then claiming the effect anyway constitutes an analytic flexibility concern and undermines the statistical basis for a key conclusion.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' yet the caption for Figure 1 states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are different thresholds (0.05 vs. 0.01). The figure caption implies a stricter threshold is used for interpreting all paths shown, while the Methods specifies the more lenient threshold. Readers cannot determine which threshold was actually applied, and some findings described as significant under p < .05 (e.g., RWA→WILL path at p = .001) would pass both, but the inconsistency creates ambiguity about the interpretive standard and may affect which borderline findings are reported or emphasized.
issues.quote: we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. [...] All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The authors use a standard (stationary) cross-lagged panel model. It is well established in the methodological literature (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015) that traditional CLPMs confound between-person trait-like differences with within-person change processes. Specifically, the cross-lagged paths in a standard CLPM capture a mixture of between-person rank-order correlations and within-person temporal effects, making it impossible to determine whether the observed lagged effects reflect genuine within-person change or merely stable individual differences. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) partitions these components and is now the recommended approach for longitudinal analyses of this type. The authors do not acknowledge this limitation, which is particularly consequential given that SDO and RWA are posited as stable trait-like attitudes.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion in five-wave longitudinal study with unreported attrition
issues.description: The paper uses listwise deletion to handle missing data in a five-wave longitudinal study spanning five years. Listwise deletion produces unbiased estimates only under the assumption that data are missing completely at random (MCAR), which is almost never satisfied in longitudinal research where dropout is systematically related to participant characteristics. Critically, the authors do not report attrition rates at any time point, deferring entirely to 'the NZAVS website.' With five waves over five years, substantial attrition is expected, and if those who drop out differ systematically on SDO, RWA, or environmentalism, the parameter estimates will be biased. Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation would be far more appropriate and are readily available in Mplus.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: In a five-wave longitudinal study from 2009 to 2013, participant retention is a critical piece of information for evaluating internal validity, selection effects, and the representativeness of the analytical sample. The paper provides no attrition figures, retention percentages per wave, or comparison of completers vs. non-completers on baseline variables. The only reference is to 'the NZAVS website' for 'retention.' This is insufficient for peer review and for readers to assess whether dropout biases the cross-lagged estimates. Journal reporting standards (e.g., CONSORT, APA reporting guidelines for longitudinal studies) require attrition to be reported in the manuscript itself.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: standard deviation vs. standard error mislabeling
issues.description: Throughout the Results section, the variability around path coefficients is labeled 'SD' (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'; 'B = -.02, SD = .01'; 'B = -.04, SD = .002'). In the context of reporting regression or path coefficients, the appropriate quantity is the standard error (SE) of the estimate, not the standard deviation. These are fundamentally different: SD describes dispersion of a variable's values, while SE describes the precision of a parameter estimate. Labeling SE as SD is a conceptual and reporting error that could confuse readers and raises questions about whether the correct statistic was extracted from the output.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: Several reported confidence intervals are inconsistent with their corresponding point estimates and standard errors. For example: (1) RWA→WILL: B = -.02, SE = .01, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]. If symmetric, the expected CI would be approximately [-.04, .00], not [-.05, -.01]. (2) WILL→SDO: B = -.04, SE = .002, 95% CI [-.04, -.03]. The lower bound equals the point estimate, which is impossible in a symmetric interval. (3) WILL→RWA: B = -.01, SE = .002, 95% CI [-.01, -.003]. Again, lower bound equals B. (4) RWA→SDO: B = .02, SE = .003, 95% CI [.02, .03]. Lower bound again equals B. These patterns suggest rounding errors, transposed bounds, or reporting from a different model than the one described.
issues.quote: The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant and negative (B = -.04, SD = .002, p < .001, 95% CI [-.04, -.03] and B = -.01, SD = .002, p = .002, 95% CI [-.01, -.003], respectively).

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances,' implying the results reported are standardized. However, Figure 1's caption reads 'Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.' The in-text results also use 'B' (typically unstandardized) rather than 'β' or a standardized notation. These statements are contradictory, and it is unclear whether the reported values are standardized or unstandardized, making the results impossible to correctly interpret or replicate.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. [...] Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The Data Analysis section contains a verbatim repeated sentence. The paragraph opens with 'We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' and closes with 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.' These are identical statements presented as if describing sequential steps, suggesting a copy-paste error. This may indicate that a distinct methodological step was intended but omitted, and raises questions about whether the analysis was fully described.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points. Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The reliability for SDO is reported as α = .69, which falls below the conventional threshold of α = .70 considered minimally acceptable for research purposes. A six-item subscale with reliability below this threshold introduces non-trivial measurement error into the SDO latent construct, attenuating its observed associations with other variables and potentially biasing the cross-lagged estimates. The authors note reliability is 'poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used' but do not acknowledge the potential impact of this on the validity of their inferences about SDO's predictive superiority over RWA.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: The paper presents a confirmatory longitudinal study with specific directional hypotheses derived from theory and prior literature (e.g., SDO stronger predictor in general population samples; bidirectional associations; reciprocal SDO-RWA effects). No preregistration is mentioned for the hypotheses, analysis plan, or analytic decisions. Given the number of researcher degrees of freedom in a cross-lagged panel model with three constructs across five waves (choice of constraints, handling of missing data, fit index selection, threshold for significance, which comparison tests to report), preregistration or transparent reporting of deviations from an analysis plan is important. The paper provides no indication of whether the hypotheses were formed before or after examining the data.
issues.quote: We also expect the longitudinal association with environmentalism to be consistent with the majority of cross-sectional literature drawing from general population samples, and therefore show SDO to be a stronger predictor than RWA.

issues.subcategory: overreach into environmental justice and IPCC findings
issues.description: The Discussion devotes multiple paragraphs to environmental racism, environmental inequality, IPCC findings on climate vulnerability, and disproportionate burden on low-income populations. While these topics are thematically related, the study's data—attitudinal survey responses from a student sample at five time points—provide no direct evidence on any of these societal phenomena. The discussion conflates individual-level ideological attitudes with macro-level structural inequalities and empirical climate projections in a way that goes well beyond what the data can support. These sections read as advocacy rather than scientific interpretation and constitute a generalizability overclaim that misrepresents the scope of the study's contribution.
issues.quote: Bryant [35] noted that environmental racism occurs when people of colour are disproportionately exposed to environmental hazards...With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The stationary cross-lagged model constrains structural paths and residual variances to be equal across time, but this requires the measurement model to be invariant across time points (i.e., that the same construct is measured equivalently at each wave). No formal test of configural, metric, or scalar invariance is reported for any of the three constructs. This is standard practice for longitudinal SEM and is especially important here given that (a) the RWA scale is missing one item at T2, (b) a five-year study period may involve developmental changes in how items are interpreted, and (c) the entire model logic rests on valid construct comparisons across waves.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: Reference [26] reads only 'Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study.' This is missing all essential bibliographic information: year of publication or data collection, publisher or repository, URL or DOI, version or wave number, and city. An incomplete citation for the dataset that is referenced for sample details (and from which some of the data may be drawn) prevents verification, replication, or further review of the sample characteristics. This also raises a transparency issue given the inconsistency between the participant description in Methods and the NZAVS.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: five 'semesters' over five years incompatible with student pool recruitment
issues.description: The Methods states that data were collected 'across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).' Five semesters span approximately 2.5 years, not 5 years (2009–2013 = 4 academic years = ~8 semesters, or 5 annual waves). More importantly, if participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool (a requirement typically fulfilled in first year), tracking the same students for even 2.5 years of semesters would be logistically implausible, as these students would not be enrolled in intro psych for multiple semesters. This further supports the inference that the sample description in the Methods may be erroneous or lifted from a different study.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.subcategory: unaddressed third-variable confounds for bidirectional relationships
issues.description: The authors acknowledge in the Discussion that 'a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable' and name economic factors and resource scarcity as candidates. However, this acknowledgment appears after several paragraphs of confident causal interpretation and is framed as a possible 'alternative' rather than a fundamental limitation. The cross-lagged model does not include political orientation, personality traits (e.g., openness to experience), or socioeconomic status—all of which are empirically related to both SDO/RWA and environmentalism and could account for the lagged associations observed.
issues.quote: Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.

issues.subcategory: overinterpretation of asymmetric SDO-RWA cross-lagged paths
issues.description: The finding that RWA predicts change in SDO but not vice versa leads the authors to conclude that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a very strong socialization claim based on a single asymmetric cross-lagged path in a sample of ~374 students (mean age 19, predominantly Pākehā). Moreover, any socialization inference from a standard CLPM is complicated by the between/within-person confound: the asymmetry could reflect between-person rank-order correlations rather than within-person socialization processes. The conclusion substantially exceeds what can be inferred from the data.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander's are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: Figure 1 is referenced throughout the Results section and is essential for interpreting the cross-lagged model's parameter estimates. The manuscript includes only the figure caption but not the figure itself. All structural paths, stability coefficients, and cross-lagged estimates for five time points and three constructs are described as shown in Figure 1, yet without the figure readers cannot evaluate the model structure, verify the reported coefficients, or assess whether the described constraints were correctly implemented.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL). All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.subcategory: Mplus syntax and model specification details deferred to website
issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.' Deferring all replication-critical analytic details to a post-acceptance website deposit is insufficient for peer review: reviewers cannot verify the model specification, the specific constraints imposed, the handling of the missing item at T2, or the chi-square difference tests as described. Given the complexity of the stationary cross-lagged model with equality constraints and the several inconsistencies identified in the reported statistics, access to the syntax during review is essential.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.
